prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

More than a hundred dollars of them. It was pure folly. I had to find more glass things to stuff them in. Now a white and purple cloud is breathing in each corner of the room I love. Now a mass of flowers spills down my dining table— each fresh-faced, extending delicate leaves into the crush. Didn't I watch children shuffle strictly in line, cradle candles that dribbled hot white on their fingers, chanting Latin—just to fashion Sevilla's Easter? Wasn't I sad? Didn't I use to go mucking through streambeds with the skunk cabbage raising bursting violet spears?—Look, the afternoon dies as night begins in the heart of the lilies and smokes up their fluted throats until it fills the room and my lights have to be not switched on. And in close darkness the aroma grows so sweet, so strong, that it could slice me open. It does. I know I'm not the only one whose life is a conditional clause hanging from something to do with spring and one tall room and the tremble of my phone. I'm not the only one that love makes feel like a dozen flapping bedsheets being ripped to prayer flags by the wind. When I stand in full sun I feel I have been falling headfirst for decades. God, I am so transparent. So light.

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: More, Now, Didn

outputs.L1:
More than a hundred dollars’ worth of them. It was sheer folly. I had to find more glass vessels to hold them. Now a white-and-purple cloud breathes in every corner of the room I love. Now a profusion of flowers spills down my dining table—each fresh-faced, extending delicate leaves into the crush. Did I not watch children shuffle in strict lines, cradling candles that dripped hot white wax onto their fingers, chanting in Latin—all to shape Sevilla’s Easter? Was I not sad? Did I not once tramp through streambeds while skunk cabbage thrust up its bursting violet spears? Look: the afternoon dies as night begins in the heart of the lilies, smoking up through their fluted throats until it fills the room and my lights need not be switched on. And in the close darkness, the fragrance grows so sweet, so strong, that it could slice me open. It does.

I know I am not the only one whose life is a conditional clause suspended from something to do with spring, and one tall room, and the trembling of my phone. I am not the only one whom love makes feel like a dozen flapping bedsheets being torn by the wind into prayer flags. When I stand in full sun, I feel as though I have been falling headfirst for decades. God, I am so transparent. So light.
outputs.L2:
Over a hundred dollars’ worth of flowers. Absurd extravagance. I had to hunt for more glass containers to crowd them into. Now, in every corner of the room I adore, a white-and-purple mist seems to exhale. Now blossoms tumble across my dining table in a heap, every one of them bright and newly opened, pushing tender leaves into the press.

Hadn’t I seen children move in rigid single file, carrying candles that dropped hot white wax onto their fingers, singing in Latin, all to create Easter in Sevilla? Hadn’t that made me sorrowful? Didn’t I once tramp through muddy streambeds where skunk cabbage thrust up exploding purple spikes?

Look: afternoon collapses as night starts inside the lilies, darkening and rising like smoke through their ridged throats until it overtakes the room and I can leave my lamps unlit. In the near-dark, the scent becomes so sweet and so powerful it feels capable of cutting me open. And it does.

I understand I am not alone in having a life that feels like an unfinished condition, suspended from something involving spring, a high-ceilinged room, and the quiver of my phone. I am not the only person whom love turns into a dozen bedsheets snapping in the air, torn by wind into prayer flags.

When I stand under direct sunlight, it feels as though I have been plunging headfirst for years and years. God, I am so see-through. So weightless.
outputs.L3:
The speaker considers it foolish to spend more than a hundred dollars on flowers, an extravagant and impractical gesture. Yet, despite this judgment, they do it anyway, filling the room with blooms until the space is completely altered. What might have seemed wasteful becomes unavoidable, almost necessary, as if the flowers answer a need the speaker cannot fully explain.

Once arranged in the room, the flowers transform everything around them. They bring in vivid color and overwhelming abundance, but also a kind of darkness and heaviness. Their presence is not merely decorative; it is immersive. The lilies, in particular, fill the air with a powerful sweetness, a fragrance so intense that it seems to press against the speaker. The room becomes saturated with spring, beauty, and excess.

This abundance of flowers draws the speaker into memory. They recall past rituals of spring, especially Easter processions, with their religious solemnity and seasonal brightness. They also remember wandering through streambeds, suggesting a more private and natural connection to spring. These memories blend ceremony, childhood, landscape, and renewal, creating a sense that spring has always carried emotional force for the speaker.

Yet the beauty of spring is not simple comfort. Its intensity exposes the speaker’s sadness, longing, and vulnerability. The fragrance of the lilies and the fullness of the season seem to strip away defenses, making the speaker newly aware of grief and desire. What begins as an act of filling a room with flowers becomes an encounter with the speaker’s own emotional depths.

At the center of this experience is love. Love makes the speaker feel delicate and unstable, as if they are being torn by wind or lifted out of their own body. It leaves them weightless, fragile, and unprotected. The speaker describes the feeling as a kind of long fall, as though they have been falling not for moments, but for decades. Love, in this vision, is beautiful and devastating at once: it transforms the world, but it also leaves the self exposed.
outputs.L4:
In spring, longing arrives before anything else. It comes before the first warm day, before the trees have fully opened their green hands, before the flowers lift their faces out of the damp earth. It begins as a scent in the dark, a sweetness almost too faint to name, and then it grows until it fills the room, the garden, the body. One remembers, suddenly and helplessly, what it is to want.

There are flowers that seem made not for decoration but for confession. Lilacs leaning over a fence, their purple clusters heavy with rain. Hyacinths breathing out their dense perfume from a windowsill. Roses still closed in their buds, guarding the red weather inside them. To stand among them in spring is to feel surrounded by small, fragrant urgencies, each bloom opening with an intimacy that feels almost indecent. Their beauty does not remain politely outside the self. It enters through the senses and unsettles everything.

Love is like that. It does not always announce itself with grandeur. Sometimes it begins as a ritual: lighting a candle at dusk, washing one’s hands, arranging flowers in a vase, waiting for someone’s footsteps or voice. The gestures are simple, but they become charged with meaning. A cup left on a table, a door not fully closed, a ribbon, a letter, a shadow moving across the wall—each object seems to tremble with possibility. When one is in love, the world becomes ceremonial. Even ordinary darkness feels prepared, as if it has been waiting to receive a secret.

And yet the sweetness of it can be nearly unbearable. Desire does not simply delight; it exposes. It makes the heart feel visible, as though the body has become translucent and every hope, every fear, every hidden tenderness can be seen. The scent of flowers at night can seem too rich, too intimate, pressing against the throat. A beautiful face, a remembered touch, the sound of a name spoken softly—these things can bring not comfort but a strange ache, because they reveal how much has been given over to another person.

In such moments, the self feels both enlarged and diminished. Love makes one weightless, lifted out of ordinary life, yet it also removes every defense. It is a kind of transformation that feels close to danger. One becomes porous, open to weather, memory, music, fragrance, silence. The boundary between the body and the world grows uncertain. A garden in bloom is no longer merely a garden; it is a mirror of the soul’s unrest. The flowers flare and fade, and in their brief intensity they resemble every human desire: radiant, vulnerable, doomed to pass, and therefore all the more precious.

Spring remembers what the heart tries to forget. It returns each year with its soft violence, its green insistence, its invitation to feel too much. In the darkness, among the flowers, longing becomes almost holy—not because it is gentle, but because it strips the self down to its most fragile truth. To love is to be changed by beauty until beauty hurts. It is to stand in the scented night, trembling, and understand that desire has made you both more alive and less protected than before.
outputs.L5:
**More, Now, Didn**

Now is the moment when everything begins to change. People often wait for the perfect time, believing they need more confidence, more experience, or more certainty before they take action. But the truth is that waiting does not always bring clarity. Sometimes, progress starts when we decide to move forward even though we didn’t feel completely ready.

We all have moments when we look back and think, “I didn’t try hard enough,” or “I didn’t take the chance when I had it.” These thoughts can be painful, but they can also become powerful lessons. They remind us that life is not only about what happened before, but about what we choose to do now.

If we want more from life—more growth, more meaning, more happiness—we must begin with the present. Now is the only time we truly control. The past didn’t define us completely, and the future has not arrived yet. What matters most is the decision we make today.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a lyrical prose poem in first person about buying too many lilies, filling an apartment with them, and being overwhelmed by their scent into memories of Easter processions, childhood spring, longing, and love.
counterfactuals.output:
I bought too many lilies because I could not stop saying yes to their white throats, their green spears, their pollen like little suns staining the air. I carried them home in my arms like a sheaf of bells, the stems knocking softly against my ribs, and filled every jar, every chipped cup, every patient glass in the apartment until the rooms stood blooming around me, altar after altar.

By evening the lilies had opened their mouths.

Their scent rose thickly from the tables and windowsills, from the floor beside my bed, from the blue pitcher in the kitchen, and the apartment became a chapel I had not meant to enter. I moved through it slowly, almost ashamed, breathing in that honeyed, funereal brightness, that sweetness with a blade hidden inside. It found the places in me I had not dusted in years.

I remembered Easter processions: the street washed clean by morning rain, girls in white socks and patent shoes, the heavy gold of the cross swaying above us, my mother’s hand warm around mine. I remembered petals bruised underfoot, wax melting down the sides of candles, the priest’s voice lifting and falling like a bird trapped beneath the rafters. I remembered being small enough to believe that spring was a door God opened with both hands.

The lilies pressed closer.

They brought back the first green afternoons of childhood, mud on my knees, light dripping from the trees, the impossible courage of crocuses shouldering through cold ground. They brought back the ache of wanting before I knew what wanting was: to be chosen, to be seen, to be held past the moment of holding. They brought back love, not one love but all of it—the letters never sent, the mouths I had missed, the names that still moved under my skin like fish beneath ice.

All night I lay awake among them. The air was crowded with their pale breathing. I thought of every goodbye that had ever worn the face of a beginning, every resurrection that had asked first for a grave. The lilies burned in the dark, invisible and insistent, and I could not tell whether they were blessing me or burying me.

By morning, pollen had fallen on the table like gold dust, and the apartment smelled of churches, rain, and open earth. I stood barefoot in the kitchen, overwhelmed, beloved by too much fragrance, and understood that longing too has a flower: it opens without permission, it fills the house, it leaves its color on everything it touches.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a contemporary personal essay fragment in a poetic, confessional style: the speaker has spent over $100 on flowers and reflects on Sevilla Holy Week, skunk cabbage, darkness, phone anxiety, and the painful lightness of being in love.
counterfactuals.output:
I have spent one hundred and twelve dollars on flowers this week, which is to say I have paid rent to beauty, or made a small bribe to the part of myself that still believes in altars.

Tulips, mostly. A bundle of ranunculus like little paper brains. One stem of something blue I could not name and therefore trusted. I carried them home in the crook of my arm with the solemnity of a woman carrying bad news. All the way up the stairs I thought of Sevilla during Holy Week, though I have never been there at the right time, only seen photographs: the penitents in their pointed hoods, the gold weight of the pasos, the Virgin so jeweled and sorrowful she seems less like a mother than a wound being paraded through the streets. Candles dissolving themselves into the night. Brass bands pushing grief forward note by note. Everyone watching. Everyone faithful, or pretending beautifully.

I understand that kind of ceremony now. How sometimes you need an entire city to move slowly around your pain.

Here, it is only me and the grocery-store flowers. Me and the sink full of stems. Me trimming each green end at an angle as if preparing them to drink from a world that has not been kind. Outside, the thaw has started to expose what winter hid. In the swampy places behind the trail, the skunk cabbage has begun its obscene little resurrection, pushing up from the muck like a dark tongue. It generates its own heat, I read once. It melts the snow around itself. Imagine being that determined to live.

I keep my phone face down on the table because every silence from it feels intentional. Because every buzz is either not you, which is cruelty, or you, which is worse. I am too old to be held hostage by a rectangle of glass. I am too old to feel my whole body become a lit room when your name appears. And yet.

This is the embarrassing part of love, how it makes a teenager of the soul. How it takes a person who has survived funerals, airports, dental surgery, tax forms, the long gray corridors of ordinary loneliness, and reduces her to someone waiting for three dots to bloom on a screen.

Darkness falls early still. Or maybe I invite it in early. By six, the windows are black mirrors and the flowers are luminous in their jars, extravagant and doomed. I move from room to room turning on lamps, trying to make a weather I can survive. The apartment fills with the faint green smell of cut stems, that tender rot already beginning.

Being in love has made everything too light to hold. That is the strangest pain of it. Not heaviness, not exactly. Lightness. The way my chest lifts and lifts until it hurts. The way hope becomes a helium thing, bright and humiliating, pulling at the wrist. I want to be dignified. Instead I am airborne and afraid.

Some nights I think of those processions in Sevilla, the hooded figures carrying their candles through streets dense with incense and human breath, and I envy them their choreography. Kneel here. Rise here. Weep here. Follow the Virgin. Follow the cross. Follow the band into the blue-black hour.

No one tells you what to do when joy is the thing that frightens you.

So I buy more flowers. I let them open. I let them die where I can see them.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a lush, sensory prose poem about spring flowers in a room, using long cascading sentences, rhetorical questions, religious imagery, and a mood of ecstatic sadness.
counterfactuals.output:
The room is full of spring flowers, and yet who has opened the window to such sorrow, who has let in this soft invasion of petals and green stems, this trembling choir of hyacinth, tulip, narcissus, and lilac, each lifting its small chalice of color as if the air itself were a chapel and the late afternoon light were pouring down the nave in honeyed sheets, touching the table, the cracked blue vase, the dust on the sill, the hands folded uselessly in the lap, as though blessing everything that is already vanishing?

O radiant arrivals, O tender perishable saints, how bravely you burn in your bowls of water, how extravagantly you spend yourselves, bruising the room with sweetness, the lilacs breathing purple dusk, the daffodils blowing their golden trumpets toward no heaven I can see, the tulips bending their waxen heads like penitents too beautiful to be forgiven, and the hyacinths—those dense censers of perfume—swinging invisibly through the air until the heart, poor worshipper, kneels without meaning to.

Is this not a resurrection, and is it not also a farewell?

For every blossom seems to rise from some buried silence, carrying the dark in its throat, the black soil still dreaming beneath its bright annunciation, and though they stand here in pitchers and jars, gathered on the sideboard like offerings for a feast, there is something funeral in their abundance, something of candles guttering around a beloved face, something of lilies laid upon a threshold no one can cross twice, and still—still—they are so lavish that grief itself grows petals, and the soul, wounded by fragrance, begins to sing.

The room becomes impossible to remain merely human in: the walls dissolve into orchard mist, the ceiling floats away like a pale altar cloth, and everywhere the blossoms lean toward one another whispering scripture in pollen and sap, saying behold, behold, the world returns, and behold, it leaves; behold the flesh made flower, the flower made breath, the breath made ache, the ache made praise.

Who could bear such mercy?

The pink blooms loosen, the white petals shine as if rinsed in moonlight, a single stem drops its head with the exhausted grace of a martyr after ecstasy, and I sit among them, dizzy with incense and loss, wanting to gather them all back into bud, back into rain, back into the secret earth before beauty had to become visible and therefore doomed, yet loving them more because they are doomed, because their splendor is a door that opens only while closing, because spring, with its green hands and tear-wet mouth, keeps entering the room like an angel who has forgotten whether it came to comfort or to announce the end.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: I want a passage that sounds like literary nonfiction crossed with poetry, narrated by someone arranging lilies and purple-white flowers at home while spiraling into memories of candles, Latin chants, streambeds, and romantic vulnerability.
counterfactuals.output:
I cut the lilies at an angle beneath the kitchen tap, their stems giving way with a green, wet sigh. The water clouded faintly, as if it had remembered earth. On the table, the purple-white flowers waited in their paper sleeve—each face bruised with violet at the throat, each petal paling toward the edge, like breath on glass. I did not know their name. I liked them better for that. They could remain untranslated.

The house was quiet except for the small domestic liturgy of scissors, vase, water, leaf stripped from stem. I arranged and rearranged them, turning the vase a little toward the window, then away. Lilies are impossible to place without making a declaration. They enter a room the way incense enters a church: slowly, then all at once, claiming the air as if the air had been waiting to be claimed.

Their scent opened something in me.

Candles first. A row of them guttering in red glass, each flame bent in a draft no one could feel. Wax collecting in soft, collapsed collars. My own hands, younger then, clasped too tightly, though I was not praying so much as listening. Latin moved above us like weather: *Kyrie eleison*, the syllables dim and gold, less understood than absorbed. I remember the mouths of the choir, the old stone sweating cold through my shoes, the sense that longing could be given architecture and then called holy.

I remember, too, the streambeds after rain: slick stones, roots exposed like the veins of a wrist, water worrying over everything it could not carry away. We walked there once, you and I, pretending to look for a place to cross. Really we were waiting for courage. The alders leaned close. Mud took our footprints and softened them immediately. When you touched my sleeve, not even my hand, I felt myself become entirely permeable, all my defended country flooded at the border.

How little it takes. A flower stem. A candle memory. A language half-lost but still singing in the bones.

Now the lilies open in their glass cylinder, white trumpets tilted toward the afternoon. The nameless purple-white blossoms fill the spaces between them, tender and deliberate, like words chosen after silence. I stand before them with wet fingers and a heart made foolish by fragrance. Outside, the day goes on being ordinary—cars passing, a dog barking, someone’s radio thin through a wall—but inside, every petal is an altar, every shadow a confessional.

I think of love as I have most often known it: not as arrival, but as the moment before speaking. The throat tightening. The candle trembling. The streambed shining with stones you may or may not be able to cross.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an intense first-person meditation on flowers, fragrance, springtime, and unrequited or anxious love, ending with an image of transparency and lightness.
counterfactuals.output:
In spring I become helpless before flowers.

I tell myself it is only weather, only the old machinery of warmth returning to the earth, sap lifting in the trees, petals loosening from their green fists. But then the air changes. It gathers sweetness. It grows intimate. A branch of blossoms leans over a wall, and suddenly I am pierced by something too delicate to defend myself against.

Fragrance is the most dangerous thing because it cannot be held at a distance. A rose may be looked away from; a lilac may be passed quickly; but scent enters without permission. It finds the locked rooms. It touches the letters I never sent, the names I do not say aloud, the small humiliating hopes I thought I had buried under ordinary days. One breath, and I am again waiting for a reply, listening for footsteps, reading tenderness into pauses, inventing whole futures from a glance.

How cruel spring is, to make everything seem possible.

The flowers open with such confidence. They do not hesitate at the brink of themselves. They pour out color, pollen, perfume, as if desire were not dangerous, as if to bloom were not to risk being bruised, ignored, cut, admired for a moment and left behind. I envy them their brief, shameless abundance. I envy the magnolia, extravagant and doomed; the violet, hidden and faithful; the peony, heavy with its own heart.

And I—what do I do? I stand among them with my anxious love, my unsatisfied longing, my mind fluttering like a trapped moth against the lamp of another person’s absence. I make omens of everything. A bee lingering in a cup of gold. A petal falling before its time. The bitter green smell of crushed stems. I ask the garden questions it cannot answer: Will I be wanted? Am I too much? Have I imagined the warmth in that voice, the softness in that silence?

The wind moves through the flowering trees and they tremble as I tremble. For a moment I think the whole world is made of waiting.

Yet even this ache has a fragrance. Even longing, when broken open, releases something. I feel it rising from me—fear, desire, tenderness, shame—all of it mingling with the wet soil and the narcissus, the hyacinth’s blue insistence, the pale breath of apple blossom. I do not know whether love will return to me. I do not know whether the door will open, whether the hand will reach back, whether I am standing at the beginning of joy or only before another beautiful refusal.

But spring goes on illuminating what it cannot promise.

So I breathe. I let the sweetness enter and leave me. I let the flowers spend themselves without asking to be saved. I let my heart be a garden no one has yet chosen, still flowering, still fragrant, still trembling in the bright air—until even my longing thins, and I am nothing but a clear vase at the window, filled with transparent water and weightless light.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
